title: Spells of protection (Kern ch. 21)
hookLine: protective chants for those who keep the sutra

lines: WORDS SAID FOR WHAT THEY DO.
cards: Some words are said less for what they mean than for what they do. A lullaby hummed over a crib. A name called across a dark yard.
The words a grandmother says when someone sneezes.

Chapter twenty-one of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, is full of words like that: strings of syllables offered to the Buddha by bodhisattvas, by heavenly kings, and by a band of fierce female spirits, all to guard the people who keep this teaching.
A new week opens with them. Today's word: dharani.

teach.h: THE GIVERS RISE ONE BY ONE.
teach.b: First, the givers. One after another they rise in the assembly: the bodhisattva Medicine King, whose own story comes tomorrow, another bodhisattva, then two of the great heavenly kings who guard the quarters of the world.
Each says, in effect: here is a spell, so that no harm comes to those who preach this teaching. And each recites it. Second, the spells themselves.

They are not sentences but runs of sound, kept as sound rather than turned into meanings. The word, dharani, is explained in the tradition as something that holds: holding the teaching in memory, holding the speaker safe.
The chant works by being kept and said, the way a lullaby works on a child who understands none of the words.

Third, the fierce ones. Then come the rakshasis, female spirits known in Indian stories for doing harm, with Hariti, whom the tradition remembers as a devourer of children turned toward protecting them.
Now they stand before the Buddha, promise to guard the keepers of the sutra, and offer a spell of their own. The very beings people feared become the guards at the door. Fourth, the Buddha's answer.
What these spells protect is not treasure or territory but people: whoever keeps the teaching, reads it, and passes it on.
Protection, in this chapter, is the circle of care that gathers around someone doing that.

how: Dharanis are recited in Mahayana and Vajrayana settings, often kept in their Sanskrit-derived sounds rather than translated; in Nichiren Buddhism people chant the sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo.

o: a written vow a monk signs on the day he's ordained
a chant of syllables kept to protect and hold the teaching
a hymn of praise sung to thank the Buddha for a gift

games.q: spells of protection: tap the pairs.

s: the spells in this chapter are ordinary sentences of instruction
they are runs of sound, kept and said rather than explained.
fierce female spirits, the rakshasis, promise to protect the sutra's keepers
with Hariti they vow to guard those who preach it, and offer a spell.
the Buddha refuses the spells as superstition
in the chapter he approves each offering.

games.q: you are a rakshasi, a spirit people fear. you stand before the Buddha as this teaching is given. what do you do?
o: promise to guard those who keep the teaching
games.why: the rakshasis, with Hariti, vow to protect the keepers of the sutra and offer their own spell: the feared become the guards.

practice: If you already chant, use a protective line from your own tradition; Nichiren Buddhists, for example, chant this sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo.
If you don't, choose a line from this path you already carry, like I do not despise you, and say it softly on each out-breath. Don't reach for meaning; just keep the line, the way a dharani is kept.

wordCard.voice: Dharani. A chant of syllables kept and recited for protection and for holding the teaching, offered in the Lotus Sutra to guard its keepers. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a chant of syllables kept for protection and for holding the teaching in memory.

carryVoice: Your line: protected. Even the fierce ones, once feared, became the guards at the door. Until tomorrow.
